entries.label: Why Hometap?
entries.value: I'm drawn to Hometap because the product has a concrete user with a real decision attached to it. A homeowner deciding whether to access equity is making a financial choice with consequences, and the software around that choice has to be correct, understandable, and trustworthy. That's the kind of problem I keep coming back to. When I built ClarityAtlas, an iOS health app I shipped into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, the hardest part wasn't estimating sleep from phone motion and HealthKit signals; it was presenting that estimate so users could actually reason about their own behavior instead of just staring at a number. Same instinct behind my job-application agent, where I architecturally blocked free-text and demographic fields from being auto-filled because a wrong action there has a real cost to a real person. A full-stack co-op at a fintech company building for homeowners puts me close to that boundary again: backend correctness on one side, a person making a decision on the other. I also want to work somewhere I'd own a meaningful piece of a system rather than isolated tickets, and a co-op on a team this size seems like it offers that.

Additional Information
entries.value: A few things that may be useful. I'm a U.S. citizen, authorized to work in the United States, and I won't need visa sponsorship now or in the future. I'm an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins studying Applied Mathematics & Statistics and Economics, class of 2029, so a spring co-op fits the way I already work: I learn by building and shipping rather than by coursework alone. On the full-stack side, I've built and run production-shaped systems end to end. For a job-application agent I wrote in TypeScript and Node, I used SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when application state diverges across processes, and I put every mutating capability behind fail-closed environment flags that never default on. I also built a React and Express operator console for running and approving that pipeline. Earlier, I founded SnapSort, an AI photo-sorting product built on Flask and AWS that grew past 300 users and raised about $5,000 in non-dilutive funding. The recurring lesson from both is that a technically functional system and a product people actually use are very different things.
